title: Stopping Fraudulent Payments Act
official_title: To amend title 31, United States Code, to authorize pausing and segmenting payments, and for other purposes.
likelihoodReason: Introduced by Rep. Comer (R-KY) with Rep. Arrington (R-TX) and 2 cosponsors; passed the House. Payment-integrity measures aimed at fraud tend to attract bipartisan support, though the bill has not yet received a Senate vote.
summary: Lets federal agencies and the Treasury pause or split up payments that show signs of fraud, while requiring payees to be notified and given a chance to contest, with the payment due within 30 days.
brief: Authorizes agencies and the Treasury to pause or segment federal payments flagged for fraud risk, with payee notice and time limits.

items.main: Names the Act the “Stopping Fraudulent Payments Act”.
items.detail: Short-title section — citation name only; no substantive effect.

sections.label: Section 2 — Authority To Pause and Segment Payments

items.main: Authorizes agencies and the Treasury to pause, condition, or segment federal payments that present an elevated fraud risk.
items.detail: Adds Section 3337 to title 31. Before certifying a payment voucher, an agency must temporarily delay, condition, or segment a disbursement that an official determines presents an elevated risk of fraud or improper payment, or when ordered by the Treasury. The Treasury may return a certified voucher and issue a corrective-action order based on a fraud-risk indicator or a Do Not Pay system flag. Actions must be objective, narrowly applied, and time-limited; the payee must be notified and given a process to contest; and the payment must be issued within 30 days of the determination (or 7 days after the payee contests). Routine, historically consistent payment amounts may proceed while an anomalous portion is held. Law-enforcement exemptions and good-faith liability protection apply, and the Treasury must issue implementing regulations within 180 days. The Treasury must also report to Congress 18 months after enactment, and annually thereafter, on the number of orders issued, the share of paused payments ultimately paid, and total savings, and the amendments take effect 1 year after enactment.

gaps: The bill sets a 30-day limit to issue a paused payment but does not specify a consequence if an agency misses it.
It relies on 'fraud-risk indicators' and the Do Not Pay system but does not address erroneous flags that wrongly delay legitimate payments beyond the contest process.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Comer
featured_quotes.text: let me translate that 5 minutes of gibberish from my colleague. They don't care about fraud. When you do find fraud, like we found in Minnesota and California, they don't want to cut off the money. They want the money to keep going so the fraudsters can stay in business. That is why we have to support this bill.

featured_quotes.name: Ms. Boebert
featured_quotes.text: I strongly support H.R. 8464, the Stopping Fraudulent Payments Act. This legislation is a commonsense, taxpayer-first bill that finally puts an end to the reckless pay-and-chase scam that has drained billions from hardworking American families. For too long, the Washington bureaucracy has operated like an open checkbook for fraudsters. They cut the checks first, ask the questions later while American taxpayers foot the bill for waste, abuse, and outright theft.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Bell
featured_quotes.text: no one in this Chamber disputes that improper and fraudulent payments are a serious problem. The question before us is not whether to fight fraud; it is how we fight fraud. If this bill actually does that--and I will give you a hint: It does not. The Stopping Fraudulent Payments Act allows agency officials to block payments whenever they have sufficient reason to believe there is an elevated risk of fraud. This bill sets the standard so low that any administration can use it to cut off legitimate recipients before a single fact is even proven.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Walkinshaw
featured_quotes.text: I will just give one agency, Social Security, an agency that has been under assault by this administration. It is estimated that 10,000 times a year, Social Security falsely declares somebody dead. Imagine that. You wake up one morning, and your own government says you are dead. It happens oftentimes because States send bad information to the Social Security Administration. Time after time after time, the IG has recommended that Social Security and this body make improvements in that process.

added: Authority for agencies and the Treasury to pause, condition, or segment fraud-risk federal payments, with payee notice and a 30-day limit (new Section 3337 of title 31)
modified: Relief of accountable officers (Section 3527 of title 31) extended to good-faith actions under the new pause authority

added: New pause trigger: agency may act on a State or local government official's notification for State-administered, federally-funded programs
Regulations must now specify the minimum seniority of the official who can order a corrective action
New agency dispute/appeal path: agencies may contest a returned voucher to the Fiscal Assistant Secretary, who must respond within five days
New Treasury report to Congress 18 months after enactment, then annually — number of orders, percentage of payments issued, total savings, and recommendations
Conforming amendments added covering payment disbursing officials (section 3325(a)(3)) and certifying officials (section 3528)
Effective date set to 1 year after enactment
modified: Pause authority broadened from agencies administering a "federally funded financial assistance or public benefit program" to the head of any agency
Treasury must issue its corrective-action order not later than 2 days after determining elevated fraud risk, tied to a Do Not Pay system output under section 3354
Payee notification must now be given within 2 days of the determination or notification (previously "prompt notice" with no deadline)
Payment-issuance deadline shortened from 45 days to 30 days after a corrective-action determination
Fraud-risk determinations now must be made "in accordance with the statutorily-defined eligibility requirements" of the program
False Claims Act reference rewritten to cite sections 3729 through 3733 of title 31
removed: Drops the Do Not Pay "flagged payee" as a standalone Treasury trigger and the separate reference to other Treasury payee-validation programs in subsection (b)
